name: Bartholomae's Law
statement: In Indo-Iranian, an obstruent cluster containing a voiced aspirate became voiced and aspirated throughout, with aspiration surfacing on the last stop.
meaning: Bartholomae's law governs how clusters of stops (and the sibilant *s) behave in Indo-Iranian when one member is a voiced aspirate. Instead of the aspirate simply devoicing next to a voiceless stop, the whole cluster assimilates to voiced and aspirated (breathy), and the aspiration is realized at the end of the cluster. It is most transparent in Sanskrit.
mechanism: A voiced aspirate plus a following voiceless stop yields a voiced cluster with aspiration retimed onto the final stop, rather than a voiceless cluster. Phonetically this is often described as breathy voice (murmur) spreading across the cluster. Grassmann's law may also operate, deaspirating an earlier aspirate in the same word.

examples.text: Sanskrit buddha "awakened," from *budh-tá (root budh-): the cluster becomes voiced and aspirated, giving -ddh- rather than -tt-.
Sanskrit labdha "taken," from *labh-ta (root labh-): *bh + t becomes bdh, surfacing as -bdh-.
Sanskrit dugdha "milked," from *dhugh-tá (root duh-/dugh-): the cluster becomes voiced-aspirated -gdh-, with Grassmann's law deaspirating the initial.

whyItMatters: The law shows that aspiration and voicing can behave as cluster-wide features rather than properties of a single segment, an important result for phonological theory. It regularizes many Sanskrit participle and derivational forms that would otherwise look irregular, and it helps date the relative ordering of Indo-Iranian sound changes.
limits: The clear, productive operation is Indo-Iranian; whether it was already a Proto-Indo-European rule is debated, since Latin and Greek show different treatments of comparable clusters. It applies to obstruent clusters involving a voiced aspirate, not to single segments in isolation.
misreadings: It is not general Proto-Indo-European assimilation carried into all daughters; its unambiguous domain is Indo-Iranian. The aspiration is not lost but relocated to the end of the cluster.
origin: Christian Bartholomae, German Indo-Iranianist, first described it in 1883.

sources.text: Wikipedia's article on Bartholomae's law, giving the Indo-Iranian scope, the buddha example, and the voiced-aspirate cluster mechanism — supports the statement and examples.
Wikipedia's glossary of sound laws in the Indo-European languages, formulating that a cluster with a voiced aspirate becomes wholly voiced and aspirated — supports the statement.
